draft.title: Metonymy
card: Metonymy names something by using a thing closely linked to it. The link is one of association, not likeness.
The crown can mean a king or queen. Canberra can mean the federal government, because that is where it sits. The press can mean journalists.
Writers use metonymy to be brief and to bring in the feelings tied to the linked thing. The crown suggests power and tradition.
A metaphor is different. It compares two unlike things, such as calling a friend a rock. In metonymy the word stands in for something it is connected to.
draft.remember: Metonymy swaps a thing's name for something closely linked to it.

a.q: A reporter writes: The White House refused to comment. What is the White House standing in for?
opts: The president and the staff who work there
A building that was damaged recently
A person who is as strong as a building
A comparison between a house and a country
a.why: The White House is closely linked to the president and staff, so the name stands in for them. This is metonymy. It is not a comparison of unlike things, so it is not a metaphor.
a.clue: Think about who makes decisions there.

opts: The pen is mightier than the sword, said the teacher
Her voice was a river of warm honey, said the critic
The test was a mountain that Jo had to climb
Time crept along like a snail on a hot footpath
b.why: Pen stands for writing and sword for force, both linked to the things they name. That is metonymy. The river of honey and mountain are metaphors, and the snail line is a simile, as each compares unlike things.
b.clue: Look for names swapped for linked things, not comparisons.

a.best: The president and the staff who work there

b.best: The pen is mightier than the sword, said the teacher

problems.detail: The clue says to look for 'names swapped for linked things, not comparisons', but the right answer, 'The pen is mightier than the sword', is itself a comparison ('mightier than'). A careful student could rule it out. The clue should say 'not comparisons of likeness' or 'not metaphors or similes'.
